world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Stress is fully contrastive in Tetun; e.g. /'kabas/ 'cotton, thread, yarn' versus /ka'bas/ 'shoulder', /'kaben/ 'marry' versus /ka'ben/ 'saliva'. Nevertheless it falls most commonly on the penultimate syllable; e.g. /ha'karak/ 'want', /ka'miza/ 'shirt'. Final stress occurs in both native and loaned items; e.g. /ha'ris/ 'bathe', /si'nal/ 'sign'. Antepenultimate stress is much less common and is found only in a small number of Portuguese loanwords; e.g. /'mediku/ 'doctor', /a'merika/ 'America'. Unstressed vowels are always short, as are non-final stressed vowels ... However, all vowels, regardless of height or quality, are regularly lengthened in stressed monosyllables and stressed final position

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default/regular stress on the penultimate syllable of the word. A minority of native words carry final stress with a lengthened final vowel (kabás 'shoulder', harís 'bathe', haré 'see'); the same author's Peace Corps course (p. xvii fn. 1) and Albuquerque 2011 / Greksáková 2018 treat these as final double vowels (kabaas, haree), under which analysis native stress is exceptionlessly penultimate (by vowel/mora count) and only Portuguese loans deviate. Antepenultimate stress exists only in a small set of Portuguese loans (médiku, siénsia), and many speakers regularise loans to penultimate. PL-528 itself labels stress 'fully contrastive' because it writes the final long vowels as single stressed vowels; hence reading fixed-penult with lexical exceptions rather than free stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: PL-528: compounds have a single primary stress like single words (sec. 4.4.1). Albuquerque 2011 sec. 6.3.1: in some reduplications/compounds a secondary stress falls on the penult of the first member, primary stress on the (penult of the) last member. Nothing on rhythmic secondary stress in long words.
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress in some native and loan words (kabás, kabén 'saliva', harís, sinál) with vowel lengthening; antepenultimate stress only in a few Portuguese loans (médiku, Amérika, siénsia, régua); unstressable clitics/particles (la 'not', preposition ba, ó '2sg'); laós with stress on o or level stress; loan stress often shifted to penult by speakers with little Portuguese (Albuquerque 2011 p. 92; Greksáková 2018 p. 311; Avram 2021 p. 93). Possible marginal vowel-length contrast flagged as needing investigation (PL-528 p. 12).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in citation forms (phonemic transcriptions of isolated words); orthographic convention marks non-penultimate stress with an acute accent. Compounds form one stress domain with a single primary stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All quoted sources describe Tetun Dili = Tetun Prasa (tetu1246, ISO tdt), the Portuguese-influenced lingua franca of Dili, as distinct from Tetun Terik/Fehan (tetu1245). PL-528 and the Peace Corps course say 'Tetun' but explicitly mean Tetun Dili; Albuquerque 2011 and Greksáková 2018 use 'Tetun Prasa'. Greksáková's PDF is held under the tetu1245 folder on file but its ch. 7 phonology is Tetun Prasa (tetu1246). Avram 2021 sec. 9 opens 'In Tetun Terik' but the cited pages and examples are Tetun Dili (apparent slip).

sources.note: Sec. 2.3 'Stress and vowel length' p. 12: stress is 'fully contrastive' (/'kabas/ 'cotton' vs /ka'bas/ 'shoulder') but 'falls most commonly on the penultimate syllable'; final stress occurs in native and loan items (/ha'ris/ 'bathe'); antepenultimate stress only in a few Portuguese loans (/'mediku/); stressed final and monosyllabic vowels are lengthened. Sec. 1.5 p. 7: 'Stress is contrastive, but usually penultimate.' Sec. 1.6: orthography marks non-penultimate stress with an acute. Sec. 4.4.1: compounds carry a single primary stress.

sources.citation: Avram, Andrei A. 2021. Contact-induced variation in Tetun Dili phonology. Acta Linguistica Asiatica 11(1): 76-98.
sources.note: Sec. 9 'Stress placement' p. 93 (second-hand, citing Williams-van Klinken et al. 2002a p. 12, Costa 2011, Albuquerque 2011): stress falls mostly on the penultimate syllable, word-final stress also attested; Portuguese loans introduced antepenultimate stress (múzika, polísia); many speakers shift loan stress rightward to the penult, attributed to East Timor Portuguese.

sources.citation: Greksáková, Zuzana. 2018. Tetun in Timor-Leste: the role of language contact in its development. PhD thesis, Universidade de Coimbra. hdl 10316/80665.
sources.note: Sec. 7.5.1 p. 311: 'In native words, stress is always on the penultimate syllable' (hemu ['he.mu], hamutuk [ha.'mu.tuk]); in borrowings stress can be final, penultimate or antepenultimate, Portuguese loans keeping original stress, marked with acute in official orthography when not penultimate; speakers sometimes shift loan stress to the penult.

sources.citation: Williams-van Klinken, Catharina. 2015 [1st ed. 2003, Glottolog 'Tetun Language Course']. Peace Corps East Timor Tetun Language Course, 3rd edition. Dili: Peace Corps East Timor (front matter + ch. 1-5 PDF from DIT).
sources.note: p. xv: 'On native Tetun words, stress is always on the second-last syllable; e.g. Uma, haTEne, haREe.' p. xvii 'Stress and long vowels': most words stressed on the penultimate syllable; some words stressed on the last vowel, spelled as double vowels (haree 'see' vs hare 'rice', kabeen 'saliva' vs kaben 'marry'); some Portuguese-origin words stressed on the third-last syllable (siénsia). Footnote 1: unclear whether final long vowels in Tetun Dili are one syllable or two (ha.ree vs ha.re.e); in Tetun Terik evidence favours two, making stress consistently penultimate.
